analysis.one_liner: Taxes household wealth above $50 million at 2% annually, rising to 6% for billionaires.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced March 1, 2021 with 8 cosponsors, it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new annual tax on wealth, not income. Households with more than $50 million in net assets would pay 2% a year on everything above that line, and 3% on assets above $1 billion, doubling to 6% if Congress passed a government-run health plan covering everyone. It orders the IRS to audit at least 30% of wealth-tax filers each year, sets tougher penalties for undervaluing assets, applies a 40% exit tax to rich people who renounce citizenship, and authorizes $100 billion for the IRS over a decade. Fewer than 1 in 100,000 households would pay it.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who already pay tax on every paycheck, would see the annual levy fall only on households holding at least $50 million in net assets. The bill also funds IRS enforcement and taxpayer services, which everyone who files taxes relies on, and strengthens disclosure rules aimed at hiding assets offshore.

how_it_helps.text: Only households with net assets above $50 million would owe the tax: 2% on wealth between $50 million and $1 billion, and 3% on wealth above $1 billion, rising to 6% if a universal government health program is enacted [S2][S3].

The IRS would be required to audit at least 30% of wealth-tax payers every year and would receive authorized funding of $70 billion for enforcement, $10 billion for taxpayer services, and $20 billion for business system modernization from 2022 through 2032 [S2][S3].

The bill closes common escape routes: trusts with the same beneficiaries count as one taxpayer, gifts to young children stay taxable, expatriating to avoid the tax triggers a 40% rate, and financial institutions can be ordered to report asset values [S3].

Undervaluing assets carries steeper penalties: 30% for a substantial undervaluation and 50% for a gross misstatement, with the Treasury empowered to set formulaic valuation methods for assets that are not publicly traded [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Roughly the tens of thousands of American households holding at least $50 million in net assets. A household with $100 million would owe about $1 million a year; a $5 billion fortune would owe about $147 million a year. Family offices, trust and estate advisers, and offshore-structuring professionals would also lose business built on shielding large fortunes from tax.

drawbacks.text: Valuing assets that are not publicly traded, like stakes in private companies, art, and real estate, is genuinely hard; the bill directs the Treasury to invent new formulaic valuation methods, and disputes over those valuations would be a standing source of litigation [S3].

Because the tax falls on wealth rather than realized income, taxpayers with illiquid fortunes, such as founders holding shares in a company they run, could face a tax bill larger than the cash they take in that year; the bill answers this by letting the Treasury defer payment for up to five years, but deferral papers over the mismatch rather than solving it [S3].

Wealth taxes have been narrow, avoidance-prone, and repeatedly repealed in Europe; the bill tries to counter that with the exit tax, the audit mandate, and steeper penalties, but enforcement would depend entirely on the IRS actually getting the $100 billion the bill only authorizes, not appropriates [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The burden lands on a small set of the wealthiest households, and the design anticipates the standard objections: audits, penalties, an exit tax, and payment deferral for illiquid fortunes. The honest weak points are valuation of private assets and the question of whether an annual wealth tax survives contact with litigation and mobility, which is why no comparable federal wealth tax exists. The core trade is clear: a few tens of thousands of very rich households pay, and the revenue plus a better-funded IRS fall to everyone else.

outcome.mechanism: It went straight from introduction to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and it died there when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Warren introduced the bill on March 1, 2021 with seven Democratic colleagues and one Independent, Bernie Sanders [S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; no markup, vote, or further action ever followed [S5].
The Congress ended January 3, 2023 with the bill still sitting in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households with more than $50 million in net assets are better off: no annual 2-6% levy on their fortunes was ever imposed, and the IRS never received the $100 billion in enforcement funding the bill would have provided.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Ultra-Millionaire Tax Act and recruited colleagues to sign on.

for.name: 7 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Markey, Gillibrand, Whitehouse, Schatz, Merkley, and Hirono joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

against.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill up for consideration in the committee that held it.

sides.party_line_note: All nine Senate supporters were Democrats or the chamber's one Independent aligned with them, and no Republican ever cosponsored it; the Finance Committee, led by a Democrat, also never acted.

industries.note: The bill would take 2-6% of their net worth every year and audit at least 30% of them annually. The tax never took effect, so they keep their fortunes intact.

The bill targets the vehicles this industry uses to hide and discount large fortunes: treated-like-one trusts, gifts to young children, expatriation, and foreign entities. Defeat of the bill preserves that business line.

industries.industry: Wealth management and asset valuation professionals
industries.note: A wealth tax would shrink fortunes under management but create large new compliance, appraisal, and reporting work; either way the costs flow through to the same handful of very rich clients.
The bill authorizes $100 billion over a decade for enforcement, taxpayer services, and modernization. A better-funded IRS pursues wealthy tax evasion that today goes largely unexamined.
